title: Security Operations: Monitoring, Detection and Alert Triage
subtitle: Work like a security operations centre analyst: read the logs that matter, write and test detection rules in Python, look at traffic in Wireshark, and triage alerts into clear findings.
outcomes: Explain what a security operations centre does and how events become alerts and incidents
Read operating system, authentication, web server and firewall logs and find what matters in them
Analyse logs with grep and Python, and look at your own network traffic in Wireshark
Write detection rules with thresholds and time windows, and test them before they go live
Triage alerts with context, separate false positives from real incidents, and document findings
prerequisites: Basic Python (reading files, loops, dictionaries and functions) and comfort in a terminal. Python 3.10 or later and Wireshark installed; on Windows, grep is available in Git Bash or WSL, and every grep step has a Python alternative. An introductory security course, or equivalent knowledge of accounts, logs and networks, helps.
description:
A security operations centre (SOC) is where an organisation watches for trouble and decides, many times a day, what deserves a response. This course teaches that work from the analyst's chair. You'll learn which logs matter and how to read them: authentication logs, web server access logs, firewall logs and operating system event logs, and how a SIEM collects and normalises them so one search covers everything.

The labs follow one day on a payments server through a SOC's workflow. You'll find repeated failed logins with grep and Python, connect web and firewall logs to the same addresses, look at your own traffic in Wireshark, write threshold and sequence detections in Python and prove them with tests, then triage a queue of alerts using asset, scanner, staff and change records, separating real incidents from false positives and writing them up as a clear ticket. The capstone is a fresh day of logs to monitor end to end. All of it is defensive practice on sample data and your own machine.

modules.title: Security operations and the logs that matter
modules.summary: What a SOC does, how raw events become alerts and incidents, and the operating system and authentication logs that analysts read every day.

lessons.title: What a security operations centre does
objectives: Describe the purpose and work of a SOC
Explain how SOC teams are organised and measured
key_points: A security operations centre (SOC) is the team, processes and tools that watch an organisation's systems, detect threats and lead the first response, often around the clock.
Its core cycle is collect, detect, triage, investigate and respond: logs and alerts come in, analysts decide what matters, and real incidents are escalated and contained.
Many SOCs work in tiers: tier 1 analysts triage alerts, tier 2 investigate the ones that need it and coordinate the response, and tier 3 hunt for threats nothing detected and improve detections.
A SOC depends on knowing its environment: which assets exist, who owns them, which matter most and what normal activity looks like.
Teams measure themselves with figures such as mean time to detect (MTTD), mean time to respond (MTTR) and the share of alerts that turn out to be false positives.
MITRE ATT&CK catalogues attacker behaviour as tactics and techniques with IDs, such as T1110 Brute Force, which SOCs use to describe detections and spot gaps in coverage.

lessons.title: Events, alerts and incidents
objectives: Distinguish events, alerts and incidents
Classify alerts as true positives, false positives and benign true positives
key_points: An event is any recorded occurrence, such as a login; an alert is an event or pattern that a detection rule flags for a person to look at; an incident is a confirmed threat or harm that needs a response.
Detection follows a pipeline: collect logs, parse them into fields, enrich them with context, apply rules, raise alerts, then triage and investigate.

A true positive is an alert about something really malicious; a false positive flags something harmless; a false negative is an attack nothing flagged; a benign true positive is accurate but expected, such as an approved scan.
Every rule balances catching attacks against creating noise: too sensitive and analysts drown in false positives, too strict and attacks pass unseen.
An alert is only as useful as its context: which asset, how important it is, who the user is and what else that address or account has done.

lessons.title: Operating system and authentication logs
objectives: Find authentication events on Linux, Windows and macOS
Recognise the log lines that matter for account security
key_points: Ubuntu and Debian record logins, sudo use and account changes in /var/log/auth.log and the systemd journal (journalctl); Red Hat-based systems use /var/log/secure.
OpenSSH writes lines such as Failed password for deploy from 198.51.100.23 and Accepted publickey for alice from 192.0.2.10, which give the result, the account, the address and the method.

Windows records security events in its Security log: 4624 is a successful logon, 4625 a failed one, 4672 a logon with special privileges, 4720 a new user account, 4740 an account lockout and 1102 the log being cleared.
Repeated failures, logins at unusual times or from new places, and a success after many failures are classic signs of an account under attack.
Account changes, such as a new user or a user added to the sudo or Administrators group, are high-value events, because intruders use them to keep their access.

walkthrough.title: Read authentication events on your own computer

steps.do: Linux (Ubuntu): show recent SSH logins and failures, and today's sudo use, from the journal.
steps.see: Lines from sshd and sudo, or -- No entries -- if nothing happened today. On Red Hat-based systems the SSH unit is sshd.

steps.do: Linux: search the auth log file directly, which is what you'll do with sample logs in the lab.
Windows: in PowerShell run as administrator, list the latest successful and failed logons from the Security log.
steps.see: Ten events with their times, each 4624 or 4625.

steps.do: macOS: show the last hour of sudo activity from the unified log.

lab.title: Find repeated failed logins in an auth log
lab.goal: Analyse a day of authentication logs from the payments server app02: count the failed logins, find which addresses they came from and which accounts were tried, and flag every address that logged in successfully after failing.
setup: Python 3.10 or later, and a terminal (grep is available on Linux and macOS, and on Windows in Git Bash or WSL)
The starter files auth.log and failed_logins.py, in one folder

steps.do: Look at the log's first lines and count the failed passwords.
Count the failures by source address, most first.
steps.code: grep 'Failed password' auth.log | grep -oE 'from [0-9.]+' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

steps.do: List every successful login, and compare their addresses with the ones above.
steps.see: Four logins: deploy, alice, carol and bob. deploy's came from an address that had just failed six times.

steps.do: Open failed_logins.py and finish parse(): TODO 1 records each failed password and counts failures per address; TODO 2 records a successful login from an address that has failed before. The regular expressions are written for you.
Run it.
steps.see: 17 failed logins from 3 addresses, then 203.0.113.45 (9, users admin, root, ubuntu), 198.51.100.23 (6, deploy) and 192.0.2.12 (2, carol), then the logins after failures.

steps.do: Write two or three sentences for each address with failures: what it tried, whether it got in, and how urgent it is. Which one needs action first, and why?

checks.text: The failure counts are right: 17 in total, from three addresses.
Each address is reported with its count and the accounts it tried.
Logins after failures are found with their times.
The analysis picks deploy's login from 198.51.100.23 as the most urgent, and explains why carol's is probably a mistyped password.

"""Summarise failed SSH logins in an auth.log, and flag addresses that logged in after failing.

Usage: python failed_logins.py auth.log
"""

import re
import sys
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

FAILED = re.compile(r"Failed password for (?:invalid user )?(?P<user>\S+) from (?P<ip>\S+) port")
ACCEPTED = re.compile(r"^(?P<time>\S+) \S+ sshd\[\d+\]: Accepted \S+ for (?P<user>\S+) from (?P<ip>\S+) port")


def parse(path):
    """Return (failures, successes).

    failures: a list of (ip, user) pairs, one for each failed password.
    successes: a list of (time, ip, user, n), one for each successful login from an address that had
    already failed n times (n > 0); time is the line's first 19 characters, such as 2026-10-05T03:22:47.
    """
    failures, successes = [], []
    failed_so_far = Counter()
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            # TODO 1: if FAILED finds a match in the line, append (ip, user) to failures
            #         and add 1 to failed_so_far[ip]
            # TODO 2: if ACCEPTED matches the line and failed_so_far[ip] > 0, append
            #         (time[:19], ip, user, failed_so_far[ip]) to successes
            pass
    return failures, successes


def main(path="auth.log"):
    failures, successes = parse(path)
    by_ip = Counter(ip for ip, _ in failures)
    users = defaultdict(set)
    for ip, user in failures:
        users[ip].add(user)
    print(f"{len(failures)} failed logins from {len(by_ip)} addresses")
    for ip, n in by_ip.most_common():
        print(f"  {ip:<15} {n:>3}  users tried: {', '.join(sorted(users[ip]))}")
    print("Logins after failures:")
    for time, ip, user, n in successes:
        print(f"  {time}  {user} from {ip} after {n} failures")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(*sys.argv[1:])

hints: FAILED.search(line) finds the pattern anywhere in the line; m['ip'] and m['user'] give the named groups.
Use continue after recording a failure, so the same line isn't also checked for a success.
No grep on Windows? Every question can be answered from the Python script's output.

modules.title: Web, firewall and network evidence
modules.summary: Read web server access logs and firewall logs, connect them by address and time, and look at network traffic itself with Wireshark.

lessons.title: Web server access logs
objectives: Read a combined-format access log line
Recognise automated probing and password guessing in web logs
key_points: Each line of a combined-format access log records the client address, two identity fields (usually -), the [time], the request line in quotes, the status code, the bytes sent, the referrer and the user agent.
Status codes summarise each outcome: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client errors such as 401 (authentication needed), 403 (forbidden) and 404 (not found), and 5xx server errors.
Many 404s from one address within seconds, for pages the site has never had, usually mean an automated tool is probing the site rather than a person browsing it.
Repeated 401 responses to a login page from one address suggest password guessing, just as repeated failed SSH logins do.
The user agent is whatever the client chose to send, so it helps group activity but proves nothing on its own; a burst of 5xx errors in the error log can be the first sign of an attack or an outage.

lessons.title: Firewall logs and network flows
objectives: Read a ufw firewall log line
Explain what flow records show and what they leave out
key_points: Ubuntu's ufw writes blocked connections to /var/log/ufw.log, marked [UFW BLOCK], with fields such as IN (the interface), SRC and DST (the addresses), PROTO, SPT and DPT (the ports) and TCP flags such as SYN.
One address trying many different destination ports within seconds is the signature of a port scan; a firewall that blocks it has done its job, but the address is worth watching in other logs.
Blocked traffic shows what didn't get in; allowed traffic and flows show what did, so an investigation needs both.
Flow records, such as NetFlow, IPFIX and cloud VPC flow logs, summarise each connection's addresses, ports, protocol, start and end times and bytes, without its content.
Any public address receives unsolicited probes all day, so the useful questions are whether activity is aimed at you specifically and whether any of it succeeded.

lessons.title: Looking at traffic with Wireshark
objectives: Capture and filter your own network traffic in Wireshark
Explain what encrypted traffic still reveals to a defender
key_points: Wireshark captures packets from a network interface and decodes every layer, from Ethernet and IP up to DNS, HTTP and TLS.
Capture only on networks you own or have permission to monitor: captures can hold personal data, so store them securely and delete them when you're done.
Display filters narrow what's shown without discarding packets, for example dns, ip.addr == 192.0.2.10, tcp.port == 443, or tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0 for new connection attempts.
Capture filters, set before a capture starts, use a different syntax (BPF), such as port 53, and decide what's saved at all.

Most traffic is encrypted with TLS, but DNS lookups and the server name in the TLS Client Hello (tls.handshake.extensions_server_name) usually still show which sites a device talks to, unless Encrypted Client Hello is in use.
Statistics | Conversations lists who talked to whom and how much, which quickly shows the busiest or most unusual connections.

walkthrough.title: Capture and filter your own traffic

steps.do: Open Wireshark and double-click your active interface (Wi-Fi or Ethernet): the one whose sparkline is moving.
In a browser, open https://example.com, then stop the capture: Capture | Stop, or the red square in the toolbar.

Show TLS Client Hellos, then expand one: Transport Layer Security | Handshake Protocol: Client Hello | Extension: server_name. Right-click the Server Name field and choose Apply as Column.

Open Statistics | Protocol Hierarchy to see which protocols made up the capture.

"""Report on a web server's access log and its firewall (ufw) log.

Usage: python web_fw_report.py access.log ufw.log
"""

import re
import sys
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

# client identity user [time] "request" status size "referrer" "user agent"
ACCESS = re.compile(r'^(?P<ip>\S+) \S+ \S+ \[(?P<time>[^\]]+)\] "(?P<request>[^"]*)" (?P<status>\d{3}) (?P<size>\S+)')
UFW = re.compile(r"\[UFW (?P<action>\w+)\].* SRC=(?P<src>\S+) DST=(?P<dst>\S+) .* PROTO=(?P<proto>\w+) SPT=(?P<spt>\d+) DPT=(?P<dpt>\d+)")
SCAN_PORTS = 5  # distinct destination ports from one address that suggest a port scan


def not_found_by_ip(path):
    """Count the 404 (Not Found) responses for each client address."""
    counts = Counter()
    # TODO 1: open the file; for each line that ACCESS matches with status "404", add 1 to counts[ip]
    return counts


def blocked_by_src(path):
    """Return {source address: (attempts, set of destination ports)} for the BLOCK lines in a ufw log."""
    attempts, ports = Counter(), defaultdict(set)
    # TODO 2: open the file; for each line that UFW matches with action "BLOCK",
    #         add 1 to attempts[src] and add int(dpt) to ports[src]
    return {src: (attempts[src], ports[src]) for src in attempts}


def main(access="access.log", ufw="ufw.log"):
    not_found = not_found_by_ip(access)
    print("404s by client address:")
    for ip, n in not_found.most_common():
        print(f"  {ip:<15} {n:>3}")
    blocked = blocked_by_src(ufw)
    print("Blocked by the firewall:")
    for src, (n, ports) in sorted(blocked.items(), key=lambda item: -item[1][0]):
        flag = "  POSSIBLE PORT SCAN" if len(ports) >= SCAN_PORTS else ""
        print(f"  {src:<15} {n:>3} attempts, {len(ports):>2} ports{flag}")
    # TODO 3: print the addresses found by both reports, sorted, on one line like:
    #         In both logs: 192.0.2.1, 192.0.2.2


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(*sys.argv[1:])

hints: ACCESS.match(line) returns None for a line that doesn't fit; check for that before reading m['status'].
The status is text, so compare it with "404", not 404.
No DNS packets in Wireshark? Your browser may use encrypted DNS (DNS over HTTPS); run nslookup example.com in a terminal during the capture instead.

modules.title: Centralising logs and writing detections
modules.summary: How SIEMs collect and normalise logs so one search covers every system, how detection rules are designed, and how to test and tune them like code.

lessons.title: Centralising logs and SIEM concepts
objectives: Explain why logs are centralised and how they're collected
Describe what a SIEM does with the logs it receives
key_points: Logs kept only on each machine are hard to search together and easy for an intruder to erase, so SOCs forward them to a central store as they're written.
Collection uses agents on each host, standard protocols such as syslog (port 514 over UDP or TCP, or 6514 over TLS) and APIs for cloud services.

Parsing turns each line into named fields (time, source address, user, action, result); normalising maps every product's names onto one schema, such as the Elastic Common Schema or OCSF, so one search covers all sources.
Times should be stored in UTC, with every system's clock kept in step by NTP, or events from different machines won't line up.

A SIEM (security information and event management) system collects, normalises, stores and searches logs, runs detection rules across them and raises alerts and cases; examples include Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, Elastic Security and the open-source Wazuh.
Retention balances cost against need: keep enough history to investigate an incident discovered weeks later and to meet legal requirements.

lessons.title: Writing detection rules
objectives: Describe the parts of a detection rule
Design threshold and sequence detections
key_points: A detection rule states the data it reads, the condition that raises an alert, the alert's severity and what an analyst should check first.
Common kinds are matching a known-bad value (an indicator), counting past a threshold within a time window, a sequence of events such as failures then a success, and departures from normal behaviour.
Threshold rules need both a count and a window: five failed logins from one address within two minutes is unusual, while five spread across a day is ordinary.

Sigma is an open, vendor-neutral format for detection rules written in YAML, with fields for the log source, the detection logic, known false positives and a level; tools convert Sigma rules into each SIEM's query language.
Linking each rule to the behaviour it detects, such as ATT&CK's T1110 Brute Force or T1078 Valid Accounts, makes gaps in coverage easy to see.

lessons.title: Testing and tuning detections
objectives: Test detection rules with events that must and must not trigger them
Tune noisy rules without hiding real attacks
key_points: Treat detections as code: keep them in version control, review changes and test each rule before it goes live.
Test with events that must trigger the rule and events that must not, including edge cases such as exactly the threshold or just outside the window.
Run a new rule over past logs before switching it on, to see how many alerts it would have raised and how many of those were real.
Tune by narrowing rather than switching off: exclude one approved scanner or service account, record why, and review exclusions regularly so they don't hide an attack.
Never tune by loosening a rule until real attacks fit underneath it; adding context, such as known office addresses, usually separates the cases better.

"""Two detection rules over normalised login events: one JSON object per line, such as
{"time": "2026-10-05T03:20:01Z", "source": "sshd", "event": "login_failure", "src_ip": "198.51.100.23", "user": "deploy"}

Usage: python detect.py events.jsonl
"""

import json
import sys
from collections import defaultdict, deque
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

BRUTE_FORCE_COUNT = 5                          # this many failures from one address...
BRUTE_FORCE_WINDOW = timedelta(seconds=120)    # ...within this long raise a brute_force alert
SUCCESS_AFTER_COUNT = 3                        # a success after this many failures from its address...
SUCCESS_AFTER_WINDOW = timedelta(minutes=15)   # ...within this long raises success_after_failures


def when(event):
    return datetime.strptime(event["time"], "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")


def load(path):
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        return [json.loads(line) for line in f if line.strip()]


def detect(events):
    """Return alerts as (time, rule, src_ip, detail) tuples, in time order."""
    alerts = []
    window = defaultdict(deque)   # src_ip -> times of failures not yet part of a brute_force alert
    failures = defaultdict(list)  # src_ip -> times of all its failures
    for e in sorted(events, key=when):
        t, ip = when(e), e["src_ip"]
        if e["event"] == "login_failure":
            failures[ip].append(t)
            # TODO 1: add t to window[ip], then drop times from its left that are more than
            #         BRUTE_FORCE_WINDOW older than t
            # TODO 2: if window[ip] now holds BRUTE_FORCE_COUNT or more times, append the alert
            #         (e["time"], "brute_force", ip, f"{len(window[ip])} failures in 120s")
            #         and clear window[ip], so the next alert needs fresh failures
        elif e["event"] == "login_success":
            # TODO 3: count the failures[ip] times within SUCCESS_AFTER_WINDOW before t; if there are
            #         SUCCESS_AFTER_COUNT or more, append the alert
            #         (e["time"], "success_after_failures", ip, f"{e['user'] or '(web)'} after {n} failures")
            pass
    return alerts


def main(path="events.jsonl"):
    alerts = detect(load(path))
    for time, rule, ip, detail in alerts:
        print(f"{time}  {rule:<22}  {ip:<15} {detail}")
    print(f"{len(alerts)} alerts")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(*sys.argv[1:])

hints: window[ip][0] is the oldest time in the window; pop it from the left while t minus it is more than BRUTE_FORCE_WINDOW.
t - f gives a timedelta, which compares directly with SUCCESS_AFTER_WINDOW.
If the deploy alert says 6 failures, the web login failures aren't being counted: count every failure from the address, whatever its source.

modules.title: Alert triage and documenting findings
modules.summary: Decide quickly and consistently what each alert means, deal with false positives without blinding the SOC, and write findings that others can act on.

lessons.title: Triage: from alert to decision
objectives: Triage an alert with a consistent method
Use context to judge an alert's impact
key_points: Triage decides quickly whether an alert needs action: confirm what the alert says happened, add context, judge the impact, then close it, escalate it or investigate further.

Context answers the key questions: how critical the asset is, who the user is and whether this is normal for them, whether the address is known (an office, a partner, an approved scanner) and what else it did.
Look across sources around the alert's time: one address that was blocked by the firewall, probed the web server and then logged in over SSH tells a story no single alert does.
Prioritise by impact and confidence: a successful login after failures on a critical server outranks failed attempts that achieved nothing.
Record every decision with its reason, so the next analyst, and anyone tuning the rules, can learn from it.

lessons.title: False positives and tuning
objectives: Identify common causes of false positives
Choose the right fix for a noisy alert
key_points: Common sources of false positives include vulnerability scanners, backup jobs, administrators' routine work, misconfigured services and people mistyping their passwords.
Alert fatigue is real: when most alerts are noise, real ones get missed, so fixing noisy rules is part of a SOC's job, not a distraction from it.
A benign true positive, such as an approved scan inside its scheduled window, is closed as expected, and usually handled with a narrow exception that names the address and the time window.
Before tuning, decide whether the rule caught real but permitted behaviour or flagged the wrong thing, because the fixes differ.
Every exception should have an owner, a reason and a review date, so yesterday's approved scanner can't become tomorrow's blind spot.

lessons.title: Documenting findings and handing over
objectives: Write an incident ticket others can act on
Hand over open cases without losing anything
key_points: A good ticket lets someone who wasn't there understand and act: a summary, a UTC timeline, the evidence (log lines and searches), the assessment, actions taken and recommendations.
Separate facts from conclusions: a login from 198.51.100.23 at 03:22:47 UTC is a fact; the account was compromised is a conclusion, which needs its evidence.
List indicators of compromise, such as addresses and account names, so they can be searched for on other systems and added to detections.
Write for the reader: a short summary first for managers, technical detail after it for responders.
At a shift change, hand over each open case with its status, what's been tried and what comes next, so nothing is dropped.

project.title: Monitor a day on the shop server
project.brief: You're the analyst on duty for shop01, an online shop's internet-facing web and SSH server, for Monday 12 October 2026. You have its authentication log, web access log and firewall log, plus context: the asset list, staff and service accounts, and the scanner allowlist. Build a small monitoring pipeline in Python: parse all three logs into one normalised event format, write at least three detection rules with tests, run them over the day, and triage every alert they raise using the context files. Somewhere in the noise is one real incident. Find it, write it up as an incident ticket, and recommend how to tune any rule that was noisy.
deliverables: Python parsers that turn the three logs into one JSON Lines file of normalised events
At least three detection rules (for example brute force, success after failures and port scan) with passing tests
The alerts your rules raise on the day's logs
A triage decision for every alert, with evidence and action
An incident ticket for the real incident: summary, UTC timeline, evidence, indicators, assessment and actions
Two or more tuning recommendations, each narrow and with a review date

rubric.name: Parsing and normalisation
rubric.description: All three logs are parsed into consistent fields (UTC time, source, event, address, user), with no lines silently lost.

rubric.name: Detections and tests
rubric.description: At least three rules with clear thresholds and windows; tests cover triggering, not triggering and edge cases, and all pass.

rubric.name: Triage
rubric.description: Every alert is decided correctly with evidence: the authorised scan, the developer's mistyped password and the failed guessing are separated from the real incident.

rubric.name: Incident ticket
rubric.description: The backup account's login from 198.51.100.61 is connected to the earlier port scan and web requests and the archive made with sudo, with a UTC timeline, indicators and sensible actions; facts are kept apart from conclusions.

rubric.name: Tuning and clarity
rubric.description: Tuning is narrow and reviewable, not loosening rules wholesale; the write-up is clear to a manager and a responder.
